chapter.title: Lojban as we mangle it in Lojbanistan: about this book

section.title: What is Lojban?
section.para: Lojbanhistory of Loglanrelation to Lojban BrownJames Cooke Lojban (pronounced LOZH-bahn) is a constructed language. It is the younger of two languages that came out of the Loglan Project. Dr. James Cooke Brown founded the project, and in 1955 he started work on its first language, Loglan. His aim was to test the hypothesis that the language that we speak shapes the thoughts that we can think.

The goals for the language were first described in the open literature in the article Loglan, published in Scientific American, June, 1960. That article made the project well known. So did occasional references in science fiction (most notably in Robert Heinlein's novel The Moon Is A Harsh Mistress) and in computer publications. Over the following decades, the project drew dozens of workers and hundreds of supporters.

Logical Language Grouprelation to Lojban
Loglan Institute In 1987 the project divided over a question that every constructed language meets sooner or later: who owns it? Earlier, Brown founded The Loglan Institute to develop Loglan. Brown and the Institute claimed the language as their intellectual property. Their claims also covered its individual words. A large group of the project's volunteers wanted the language to be free for anyone to use. The two sides did not reach an agreement, so those volunteers formed The Logical Language Group, which later published the first edition of this book.

The volunteers rebuilt the vocabulary of the language from the ground up, but they kept its grammatical design. They made an entirely new stock of root words from the six most widely spoken languages of the world. To do this, they used the same method that gave Loglan its root words. The result is Lojban.

The dispute over the name Loglan itself went to court, and the case ended in 1992. The ruling was on narrow grounds: Loglan is the generic name of a language, so nobody can keep it as a registered trademark. Later, usage settled the names more amicably than the court case did. Today the name Loglan usually refers to the language of the Institute. People still use and develop that language, and its materials are at loglan.org. The name Lojban refers to the language of the Group.

The two are sibling languages. Their grammatical structure is alike: you can often translate a simple sentence of one language word by word into the other. But almost all of their words are different. Of the two, Lojban is now much more widely used. It is the language that this book describes.

Lojbanfeatures of
There are thousands of artificial languages (of which Esperanto is the best-known), but Lojban has been engineered to make it unique in several ways. The following are the main features of Lojban:

listitem.para: Lojban is designed to be used by people in communication with each other, and possibly in the future with computers.
Lojban is designed to be neutral between cultures.
Lojban grammar is based on the principles of predicate logic.
Lojban has an unambiguous yet flexible grammar.
Lojban has phonetic spelling, and unambiguously resolves its sounds into words.
Lojban is simple compared to natural languages; it is easy to learn.
Lojban's 1300 root words can be easily combined to form a vocabulary of millions of words.
Lojban is regular; the rules of the language are without exceptions.
Lojban attempts to remove restrictions on creative and clear thought and communication.
Lojban has a variety of uses, ranging from the creative to the scientific, from the theoretical to the practical.
Lojban has been demonstrated in translation and in original works of prose and poetry.

section.title: What is this book?
section.para:
goal of this book this bookgoal of
reference grammar This book is what is called a reference grammar. It attempts to expound the whole Lojban language, or at least as much of it as is understood at present. Lojban is a rich language with many features, and an attempt has been made to discover the functions of those features. The word discover is used advisedly; Lojban was not invented by any one person or committee. Often, grammatical features were introduced into the language long before their usage was fully understood. Sometimes they were introduced for one reason, only to prove more useful for other reasons not recognized at the time.

By intention, this book is complete in description but not in explanation. For every rule in the formal Lojban grammar (given in ), there is a bit of explanation and an example somewhere in the book, and often a great deal more than a bit. In essence,
gives a brief overview of the language,
gives the formal structure of the language, and the chapters in between put semantic flesh on those formal bones. I hope that eventually more grammatical material founded on (or even correcting) the explanations in this book will become available.

linguistic drift Lojbanstability of
Nevertheless, the publication of the first edition of this book in 1997 was, in one sense, the completion of a long period of language evolution. The Logical Language Group declared the language baselined: its official definition became a fixed reference point. Even the consideration of a revision had to wait for five years. Later events roughly followed that plan, but not its spirit of finality.

A baseline statement in 2002 started the plan. In 2003 the Logical Language Group, which was then responsible for the language, chartered a language-definition committee. Its Lojban name is BPFKlanguage-definition committee
baupla fuzykamni, or BPFK for short. Its task was to produce a definitive specification of the language. Along the way, the BPFK and the Group adopted a small number of deliberate changes to the language that this book describes. The changes with the largest consequences are these:

listitem.para: A reformed system of articles, adopted in stages between 2004 and 2020
A stricter rule for word forms (2014)
A rule that attaches a tense word, or a similar word, tightly to a following phrase that names a relation (2016)

section.para: This edition teaches the language with these changes. Where it teaches a changed rule, a note tells you who adopted the rule, when, and how firmly. With these notes, you can always tell settled rules from community practice that is still in motion.

Logical Language Groupstatus of
Lojbangovernance of
Later, deliberate change stopped. This time it stopped without a proclamation. The Logical Language Group is now effectively inactive. Its last recorded meeting was the 2022 Annual Meeting, which ended in 2023. No later activity is on record. The BPFK left its remaining open questions deferred, and they now stay deferred indefinitely.

In practice, the established core of the language is frozen. This core is the old baseline plus the later decisions that this book describes, each at its own level of authority. The language itself is not frozen.

Lojban still grows the way living languages do: through use, new vocabulary, and consensus in usage and in the tools that everyone shares. After the first edition, the community coined thousands of words by the processes that
describes, and it submitted them to the community dictionaries. All of this growth is fully decentralized. (Teach your children Lojban!)
You can learn the language that this book describes with reasonable assurance that its core will not change under you. Nobody forbids further changes, but it is now nobody's job to make them.

this bookstructure of
structure of this book It is probably worth mentioning that this book was written somewhat piecemeal. Each chapter began life as an explication of a specific Lojban topic; only later did these begin to clump together into a larger structure of words and ideas. Therefore, there are perhaps not as many cross-references as there should be. However, I have attempted to make the index as comprehensive as possible.

chapter titlesintent of
jokes Lojbanistan Each chapter has a descriptive title, often involving some play on words; this is an attempt to make the chapters more memorable. The title of
(which you are now reading), for example, is an allusion to the book English As We Speak It In Ireland , by P. W. Joyce, which is a sort of informal reference grammar of Hiberno-English. Lojbanistan is both an imaginary country where Lojban is the native language, and a term for the actual community of Lojban-speakers, scattered over the world. Why mangle ? As yet, nobody in the real Lojbanistan speaks the language at all well, by the standards of the imaginary Lojbanistan; that is one of the circumstances this book is meant to help remedy.

section.title: What are the typographical conventions of this book?
section.para: Each chapter is broken into numbered sections; each section contains a mixture of expository text, numbered examples, and possibly tables.

this bookexamples of examples in this book The reader will notice a certain similarity in the examples used throughout the book. One chapter after another rings the changes on the self-same sentences:

will become wearisomely familiar before
is reached. This method is deliberate; I have tried to use simple and (eventually) familiar examples wherever possible, to avoid obscuring new grammatical points with new vocabulary. Of course, this is not the method of a textbook, but this book is not a textbook (although people have learned Lojban from it and its predecessors). Rather, it is intended both for self-learning (of course, at present would-be Lojban teachers must be self-learners) and to serve as a reference in the usual sense, for looking up obscure points about the language.

examplesstructure of
structure of examples example of examples It is useful to talk further about
for what it illustrates about examples in this book. Examples usually occupy three lines. The first of these is in Lojban (in italics), the second in a word-by-word literal translation of the Lojban into English (in boldface), and the third in colloquial English. The second and third lines are sometimes called the literal translation and the colloquial translation respectively. Sometimes, when clarity is not sacrificed thereby, one or both are omitted. If there is more than one Lojban sentence, it generally means that they have the same meaning.

square bracketsuse of in notation
Words are sometimes surrounded by square brackets. In Lojban texts, these enclose optional grammatical particles that may (in the context of the particular example) be either omitted or included. In literal translations, they enclose words that are used as conventional translations of specific Lojban words, but don't have exactly the meanings or uses that the English word would suggest. In
, square brackets surround phonetic representations in the International Phonetic Alphabet.

grammatical categoriesuse of upper case for
tablesformat of
Many of the tables, especially those placed at the head of various sections, are in three columns. The first column contains Lojban words discussed in that section; the second column contains the grammatical category (represented by an UPPER CASE Lojban word) to which the word belongs, and the third column contains a brief English gloss, not necessarily or typically a full explanation. Other tables are explained in context.

technical terms A few Lojban words are used in this book as technical terms. All of these are explained in
, except for a few used only in single chapters, which are explained in the introductory sections of those chapters.

section.title: Disclaimers
section.para: disclaimers It is necessary to add, alas, that the examples used in this book do not refer to any existing person, place, or institution, and that any such resemblance is entirely coincidental and unintentional, and not intended to give offense.

dictionarysuperior authority of
When definitions and place structures of gismu, and especially of lujvo, are given in this book, they may differ from those given in the English-Lojban dictionary (which, as of this writing, is not yet published). If so, the information given in the dictionary supersedes whatever is given here.

From 2017 on, Gleki Arxokuna (lagleki) kept a community version of the book, known as UnCLL. It corrected errata and added new material, such as the tables of the zbalermorna script. This edition starts from that version. Ilmen, la-ninpre, mezohe, Corbin, Vexatos, and Gregorio Guidi also contributed to it.

The formal grammar of word forms in
is the work of Jorge Llambias. It comes from camxes, the parser that he and Robin Lee Powell first wrote. Masato Hagiwara ported camxes to JavaScript, and the ilmentufa project of Ilmen, Gleki Arxokuna, and others maintains the current version. The translators of the texts in
appear with each text.

The changes to the language after 1997 come from the BPFK, the Logical Language Group, and the wider Lojban community.
lists them, and this book names the source of each change where it teaches it.

Pavel Minaev started this edition in 2026 and made its editorial decisions. Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, wrote the new and changed text with him, under his direction. AI models from OpenAI, xAI, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, and Google reviewed that text. The camxes parser tests every Lojban example in the book, and jbotci, a Lojban toolkit, helped to test the new examples.

section.title: Informal bibliography
section.para: The logic of Lojban, such as it is, owes a good deal to the American philosopher W. v.O. Quine, especially Word and Object (1960, M.I.T. Press). Much of Quine's philosophical writings, especially on observation sentences, reads like a literal translation from Lojban.

The theory of negation expounded in
is derived from a reading of Laurence Horn's work A Natural History of Negation.
Of course, neither Brown nor Quine nor Horn is in any way responsible for the uses or misuses I have made of their works.

books about Lojban At this point in its text, the first edition promised three future books: a textbook, a Lojban/English dictionary, and a book of general information. What arrived instead suited the internet age better. The community built its own dictionary collection, jbovlastecommunity dictionary, read-only status
jbovlaste, which is now read-only, but the current dictionary tools carry its content forward. Free online courses and textbooks also appeared, with a steady stream of translated and original Lojban text. Any web search for Lojban finds the current versions of all of these. Because they are online, they stay more current than any printed list can.
